content.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
Calculate and interpret gradients in real-life contexts
Read values from real-life graphs and explain what they represent
Understand the difference between linear and non-linear real-life graphs

Graphs are used every day to represent real-world situations: tracking a journey on a distance-time graph, converting between currencies, monitoring temperature changes, or comparing costs. Being able to read, draw, and interpret these graphs is one of the most practical mathematical skills you will learn.

A cyclist leaves home at 9:00 am. The distance-time graph shows their journey.
From 10:00 to 10:30 they stop for a rest.
From 10:30 to 11:30 they travel a further 20 km.
Calculate the speed for each section.
The cyclist is stationary, so the speed is $0$ km/h.
The third section is steeper, confirming the cyclist was travelling faster.
A conversion graph shows that 5 miles = 8 km. Use this to convert: (a) 20 miles to km (b) 40 km to miles
On a conversion graph, you would read across from 20 on the miles axis to the line, then down to the km axis to get 32.
A graph shows the cost of printing leaflets. At 100 leaflets the cost is £30, and at 300 leaflets the cost is £50. Find and interpret the gradient.

Example 4: Return Journey on a Distance-Time Graph
A walker leaves home at 2:00 pm, walks 6 km in 1.5 hours, rests for 30 minutes, then walks back home in 1 hour. Calculate the speed of the return journey and the average speed for the whole trip.

Two friends set off on a walk at the same time. Person A walks at 5 km/h. Person B walks at 3 km/h but had a 2 km head start. After how long does Person A catch up with Person B? Set up and solve using a distance-time graph approach.

A bath is filled at a constant rate for 5 minutes, then the tap is turned off for 3 minutes, then the plug is pulled and the bath empties in 8 minutes. Sketch a depth-time graph and calculate the rate of emptying if the maximum depth was 40 cm.
A currency conversion graph passes through the origin and the point $(100, 85)$. Find the gradient and explain what it represents.
A car journey has three stages: 40 km at 80 km/h, a 15-minute stop, then 30 km at 60 km/h. Calculate the average speed for the whole journey.
Explain why a distance-time graph can never go below the horizontal axis.
First section: $\frac{30}{1} = 30$ km/h. Second section: $\frac{15}{0.75} = 20$ km/h.
Total distance $= 24 + 16 = 40$ km. Total time $= 1.5 + 0.5 + 1 = 3$ hours. Average speed $= \frac{40}{3} = 13.\overline{3}$ km/h $\approx 13.3$ km/h.
Each additional unit of electricity costs £0.15.
Person A: distance $= 5t$. Person B: distance $= 2 + 3t$. Setting equal: $5t = 2 + 3t$, so $2t = 2$, giving $t = 1$ hour.
Rate of emptying $= \frac{40}{8} = 5$ cm per minute. The graph rises linearly for 5 min, is flat for 3 min, then decreases linearly for 8 min back to 0.
Gradient $= \frac{85}{100} = 0.85$. This means £1 converts to 0.85 of the other currency (or for every 100 units of the foreign currency, you receive £85).
Time for stage 1: $\frac{40}{80} = 0.5$ h. Stop: $0.25$ h. Time for stage 3: $\frac{30}{60} = 0.5$ h. Total time $= 1.25$ h. Total distance $= 70$ km. Average speed $= \frac{70}{1.25} = 56$ km/h.
Distance from the starting point cannot be negative. The graph may come back down to zero (returning to the start), but not below.
Always check the units on both axes before reading values.
When calculating speed from a distance-time graph, make sure your time is in the correct units (convert minutes to hours if the distance is in km).
If the question asks for average speed, use total distance and total time -- do not average the individual speeds.
Show your gradient calculations clearly: write the change in $y$ over the change in $x$ with units.
For conversion graphs, read values carefully by drawing lines across and down to the axes.
